title: Bharat’s civilisational journey had, for centuries, been a story of cultural exchange: Hon’ble Prime Minister
subtitle: Brihattar Bharat to Strengthen Global Cultural Connections through Joint Research and International Collaboration:  Union Minister of Culture and Tourism Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                14 OCT 2026 8:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The three-day international conference on ‘Bharat’s Cultural Connections across the Globe’ by the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA), an autonomous institution under the Ministry of Culture, Government of India Government of India, was inaugurated by the Union Minister of Culture and Tourism, Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat. The conference is being held from 14 to 16 October 2026 at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi. Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi conveyed his best wishes for the conference through a message, which was read out by Shri Vivek Aggarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Culture. Shri Vivek Aggarwal also delivered the introductory address.
Dr. Sachchidanand Joshi, Member Secretary, IGNCA, delivered the welcome address, while Dr. Arvind Kumar, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Culture, Government of India, proposed the vote of thanks. Prof. Dharm Chand Choubey, Head of the Brihattar Bharat Division at IGNCA, was also present on the occasion. An exhibition titled ‘Asia’s Shared Cultural Heritage’ was organised during the conference. Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Shri Vivek Aggarwal and other distinguished guests visited the exhibition, which showcases the shared heritage and historical cultural connections between India and other Asian countries.
On this occasion, Shri Vivek Aggarwal read out the message of the Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. Extending his best wishes to the Ministry of Culture and the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, the Prime Minister warmly welcomed the scholars, researchers, diplomats and other distinguished participants from India and abroad attending the conference.
In his message, the Prime Minister said that India’s civilisational journey had, for centuries, been a story of cultural exchange. Centres of learning such as Nalanda strengthened the exchange of knowledge between India and other parts of Asia, while Buddhist monks, scholars, traders and travellers carried Indian ideas to different parts of the world through land and maritime routes.
He observed that this cultural dialogue continued to flourish, with Indian philosophy, music, dance, literature, cinema and culinary traditions connecting societies across the world with India. The celebration of Indian festivals and traditions in many countries, along with the global spread of yoga, exemplified how India’s ancient knowledge traditions continued to connect people across countries and cultures.
The Prime Minister noted that India’s cultural heritage was receiving increasing global recognition. He highlighted the significance of the conference in marking the centenary of the Greater India Society, which had played an important role in promoting the study and understanding of India’s cultural and intellectual relations with Asia and other parts of the world. He expressed the hope that the deliberations would further strengthen understanding of the historical and cultural ties between India and the world and advance international cultural cooperation.
Shri Gajendra Singh Shekhawat said that the Brihattar Bharat Conference provides an opportunity to explore how the wisdom of the past can guide our future and how cultural exchanges enable civilisations to share ideas, knowledge and artistic traditions. Marking the centenary of the Greater India Society, established in Calcutta on 14 October 1926, the conference reaffirms the importance of studying India’s historical and cultural connections with the world. Brihattar Bharat should be understood not as a political or territorial claim, but as a broad sphere of cultural and historical connections. He reiterated that India’s civilisational outlook, expressed through the principle that the entire world is one family, offers a lasting message of mutual respect and shared responsibility. Culture should connect the world, not divide it. Even when political relations become difficult or languages create barriers, cultural exchanges and evidence-based research can foster understanding and sustain dialogue.
He emphasised that the study of India’s global cultural connections should develop into a dynamic, evidence-based field grounded in international collaboration. Brihattar Bharat should become a platform where shared heritage inspires joint research, strengthens mutual understanding and builds enduring international partnerships. The conference should not merely commemorate a significant scholarly endeavour, but also mark the beginning of a renewed international movement to study, preserve and exchange the cultural connections that unite humanity.
Shri Vivek Aggarwal highlighted that the Brihattar Bharat Project seeks to bring India’s ancient cultural connections with the world to international recognition through collaborative, evidence-based research involving scholars from around 51 countries. Marking the centenary of the Greater India Society, the project aims to explore India’s contributions to global knowledge systems, languages, sciences, art and cultural traditions through joint research, seminars and workshops. It also envisages a structured five-year agenda for international academic exchange and seeks to explore multinational nominations of shared intangible cultural heritage to UNESCO’s Representative List. Brihattar Bharat is a joint scholarly endeavour to deepen understanding of our shared heritage and strengthen international relations. By fostering academic collaboration and cultural dialogue, the initiative seeks to carry forward a message of peace, unity and shared prosperity, rooted in the timeless Indian principle of ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’- the world is one family.
In his welcome address, Dr. Sachchidanand Joshi said that the identity of civilisations is shaped not only by geographical boundaries, but also by the journeys of ideas, the movement of people and the memories they leave behind. Throughout history, merchants crossed mountains and seas, Buddhist monks and pilgrims travelled between sacred sites, scholars exchanged ideas and translated texts, while artisans carried their skills and artistic traditions across regions. These encounters enabled cultures to engage in dialogue, learn from one another and evolve, creating connections that continue to shape the world. The concept of Brihattar Bharat is rooted in this rich history of cultural exchange.
He explained that Brihattar Bharat is an initiative of the ICR Division of the Ministry of Culture, implemented by IGNCA, to identify, document, preserve and make accessible the shared cultural heritage of Indian civilisation and selected countries. The initiative seeks to look beyond geographical and political boundaries to explore the historical connections and cultural exchanges between people across nations.
Prior to the inaugural session, a plenary session was held under the chairmanship of Ambassador Shashank (IFS, Retd.), Former Foreign Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs and Former President of Antar Rashtriya Sahayog Parishad (ARSP). The session featured Diana Mickevičienė, Ambassador of Lithuania to India; Ambassador Jagnnath Sami, High Commissioner of Fiji to India; Ms. Lily Pandeya, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Culture; and Shri T.C.A. Raghavan, former diplomat and author, as speakers. Ms. Priyanka Chandra, Director, ICR(International Cultural Relations)  Division, Ministry of Culture, moderated the session. Ambassadors and delegates participating in the conference were also present.
The conference seeks to renew the scholarly legacy of the Greater India Society through interdisciplinary research and international collaboration, exploring historical cultural exchanges between India and the world. The deliberations cover ten themes, examining shared traditions in philosophy, religion, languages, arts, textiles, cuisine, performing arts, trade and diaspora communities across regions. Organised under the Brihattar Bharat Scheme (2026–2031), the initiative aims to advance collaborative research, documentation, digitisation and preservation of shared cultural heritage. It also seeks to strengthen international academic partnerships and promote the global dissemination of research on India’s cultural connections with the world.

title: INDIAN NAVY COMPLETES MAIDEN COMMAND OF COMBINED TASK FORCE 154
date:

content:
The Indian Navy successfully completed its maiden Command of a Combined Maritime Forces (CMF) Task Force, with the relinquishment of Command of Combined Task Force 154 (CTF 154) at a ceremony held in
Manama, Bahrain, on 14 Oct 2026
. The eight-month tenure marked a significant milestone in India's growing contribution to multinational maritime training, capacity building and collaborative maritime security.
The ceremony was attended by VAdm Curt A Renshaw, Commander Combined Maritime Forces; HE Dr Pradeep Singh Rajpurohit, Ambassador of India to the Kingdom of Bahrain; Cmde Khalid Jasim Althawadi, Naval Sector Commander, Royal Bahrain Naval Force; Cmde Dan Thomas, Deputy Commander Combined Maritime Forces; and senior representatives of CMF Headquarters and Partner Nations
. VAdm Manish Chadha, Director General Naval Operations, Indian Navy, participated through video teleconferencing. During the ceremony, Cmde Milind M Mokashi, formally relinquished Command of CTF 154 and handed over responsibilities to Commander Melissa Desjardins, Deputy Commander CTF 154, who received Command on behalf of CMF Headquarters.
Established in May 2023
, CTF 154 is CMF's dedicated multinational maritime training Task Force, mandated to enhance professional competencies, interoperability and capacity development among Partner Nations. The Indian Navy assumed Command of CTF 154 on 11 February 2026, becoming the first Indian Navy contingent to lead a CMF Task Force.(
https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2226776
)
During its tenure, the Indian Navy-led CTF 154 conducted 20 Staff Enhancement Training engagements, two major multinational training exercises and the inaugural Subject Matter Expert Exchange on Piracy and Armed Robbery (SPAR 2026)
. These initiatives collectively generated over
7,800 training hours
, with personnel from
39 countr
ie
s
participating in CTF 154 activities. The Staff Enhancement Training and SPAR engagements alone recorded over 1,100 participant attendances, reflecting the scale and reach of the training initiatives undertaken during the Command.
A major highlight was
Operation Compass Rose 26-1
, conducted from
20 to 22 Apr 2026
. Adapted to a fully virtual format in view of the prevailing regional security environment, the exercise brought together 137 participants, 11 observers and 21 facilitators from 25 Partner Nations and 13 organisations. The exercise demonstrated the ability of CMF partners to sustain multinational training and operational coordination despite regional constraints.
Operation Southern Readiness 26-2
, conducted at the Southern Naval Command, Kochi, from 20 to 23 Jul 2026, marked the
first major CMF training exercise hosted by India
. The exercise witnessed participation of 276 personnel from 27 countries and generated approximately 3,800 training hours, making it the largest Maritime Domain Enhancement Training engagement undertaken by CTF 154 since its establishment. The exercise provided participating nations an opportunity to train at the Indian Navy's specialist training establishments and gain exposure to advanced simulators and operational platforms, highlighting India's established naval training infrastructure and capacity to support multinational training requirements.
(
https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2288511
)
The 20 Staff Enhancement Training engagements addressed a broad spectrum of contemporary maritime security challenges, including Maritime Domain Awareness, Maritime Law and Law Enforcement, Information Sharing, Counter-Piracy, Maritime Crime Investigation, Cyber Resilience, Emerging Technologies, Multinational Operational Planning, Leadership and Personnel Resilience. Drawing upon expertise from the Indian Navy, CMF Task Forces, Partner Nations, regional maritime agencies and specialist institutions, the programme facilitated the exchange of operational experience and specialised knowledge. Notably, the tenure witnessed the
first dedicated 'Training of Trainers' engagement within the CMF training framework
and CMF's first professional engagement with a Judge of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.
The concluding major training engagement was SPAR 2026, conducted on 05 and 06 Oct 2026
. The inaugural exchange brought together 135 participants, including facilitators, from 25 countries, with contributions from 19 organisations and specialist teams. The initiative provided a common platform for operational counter-piracy forces, maritime law enforcement agencies, Information Sharing organisations, legal specialists, technology providers and the maritime industry to deliberate upon evolving piracy threats and contemporary challenges in maritime security.
During the Command tenure, CTF 154 also expanded its engagement with regional partners and specialised institutions. Participation in the Fifth Regional Maritime Law Enforcement Dialogue at Nairobi and interactions with the Royal Bahrain Naval Force facilitated discussions on maritime law enforcement, emerging training requirements and avenues for future cooperation.
India joined the Combined Maritime Forces as an Associate Partner in 2022 and became a full member in 2023.
The successful completion of its maiden Command of CTF 154 represents an important progression in India's engagement with the multinational maritime partnership. The tenure demonstrated the Indian Navy's ability to plan, coordinate and deliver multinational training initiatives, bringing together diverse nations, institutions and operational expertise in support of shared maritime security objectives.
The successful tenure reinforces India's growing contribution to regional maritime security and underscores the Indian Navy's role as a Preferred Security and Training Partner, committed to strengthening maritime capacities and promoting a secure, stable and rules-based maritime environment.

Speaking at the launch of IIT Kanpur’s ‘Greater Than Us’ fundraising campaign in New Delhi on October 14, 2026, he emphasised that strengthening indigenous technological capabilities is strategically crucial as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, unmanned platforms, advanced sensors, cybersecurity and space-based technologies are reshaping military dynamics.

Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi-led Government’s ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ commitment lies at the centre of its ‘Viksit Bharat’ vision as it aims to create a technologically capable, economically competitive, innovative and confident nation, which is not just a consumer of knowledge & technology but an active contributor to their creation, he said.
Shri Rajnath Singh highlighted the importance of strong institutions of higher education and research in realising this vision, noting that the Government has made sustained efforts to strengthen the ecosystem, whose growing contribution to innovation and entrepreneurship is reflected in the IIT ecosystem’s support for over 6,000 start-ups, 56 unicorns and nearly 5,000 patents. “These achievements demonstrate that IITs are not merely institutions that impart knowledge, but are increasingly becoming engines of innovation, enterprise and technological capability. Institutions such as IIT Kanpur play a significant role in advancing India’s development by expanding scientific capabilities, strengthening the innovation ecosystem and creating solutions that benefit society,” he added.
Acknowledging the initiatives undertaken in this direction, Raksha Mantri made special mention of IIT Kanpur’s DRDO-Industry-Academia Centre of Excellence and welcomed the proposal to establish a School of Defence Technologies at the Institute. He added that the proposal to set up a National Military Drone Technology Hub at IIT Kanpur, in collaboration with the Ministry of Defence to fast-track indigenisation and innovation to gain combat edge, has made significant progress and its approval process is nearing completion.
Shri Rajnath Singh exuded confidence that such partnerships would bring scientific talent, institutional expertise and the operational experience of the Defence Forces under one umbrella to develop indigenous technologies of strategic importance. Credible academic institutions can play a crucial role in translating research into practical defence applications and addressing the evolving technological requirements of the military, he said.
On IIT Kanpur’s role in strengthening Uttar Pradesh’s industrial ecosystem, Raksha Mantri said that the institute can serve as a bridge between scientific research and industrial application, emerging technologies and enterprise. He noted that Kanpur’s rich industrial legacy, coupled with IIT Kanpur’s technological expertise can generate new opportunities for entrepreneurship, employment, investment and economic growth, contributing to the state’s vision of becoming a one-trillion-dollar economy.
Shri Rajnath Singh referred to the C3i Cybersecurity Technology Innovation Hub at IIT Kanpur and the institute’s medical school, terming them as significant initiatives in cybersecurity, healthcare and medical technology innovation. He stated that research in emerging areas such as advanced materials, semiconductors, quantum technology and environmental sustainability would be critical to addressing national priorities and developing future technologies.
Stressing the need for sustained investment in research and innovation, Raksha Mantri referred to the Government’s approval of Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation Scheme to catalyse private-sector investment in research & advanced technologies. “While public policy can create an enabling environment, institutions must nurture talent and generate ideas, and industry must help translate innovations into practical applications and scale them up,” he said.
Through the ‘Greater Than Us’ campaign, IIT Kanpur aims to raise US$1 billion by March 2029, which is the largest fundraising campaign ever undertaken by any IIT. Rs 4,155 crore, nearly half of the goal, has already been committed by alumni, donors, corporate partners, and the government. The objective is to strengthen IIT Kanpur’s research infrastructure, nurture talent, and accelerate the development and commercialisation of indigenous technologies & innovations to support India’s vision of becoming a developed nation by 2047.
Shri Rajnath Singh expressed confidence that the campaign would support stronger research capabilities, advanced facilities, opportunities for talented students and solutions to national & global challenges. He called upon the institute’s alumni, industry, philanthropic supporters and institutional partners to contribute through financial support, mentorship, research partnerships and professional networks.
Prof Manindra Agrawal, Director, IIT Kanpur; Shri Awanish Kumar Awasthi, Advisor to the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh and faculty, students & alumni of the institute were present on the occasion.

title: India seeks an Indo-Pacific where all countries make their own choices, protect their interests & pursue development in peace: Raksha Mantri at 1st ASEAN-India Defence Think Tank Forum
subtitle:
“Need to build trust, respect each other’s sovereignty, follow international law & keep channels of dialogue open to tackle borderless challenges”

Strengthening maritime domain awareness, interoperability & underwater cooperation is key to a stable, rule-based maritime order, says Shri Rajnath Singh

“Self-reliance does not mean working in isolation; it can create opportunities for trusted partners to design, build, maintain & improve equipment together”

“Co-development, co-production, MRO, training and long-term technical support can build local skills, support industry & make supply chains more reliable”
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                14 OCT 2026 11:44AM by PIB Delhi
content:
“India seeks an Indo-Pacific where all countries - large and small - make their own choices, protect their interests and pursue development in peace,” said Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh as he called for building trust, respecting each other’s sovereignty, following international law and keeping channels of dialogue open to tackle both emerging and conventional “borderless challenges”. He was addressing the maiden Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) - India Defence Think Tank Forum at Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (MP-IDSA) in New Delhi on October 14, 2026.
Raksha Mantri asserted that India and ASEAN share a clear interest in peace, stability, prosperity and an open & inclusive Indo-Pacific. He emphasised that India’s Act East policy and the vision of SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region) and MAHASAGAR (Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions) advocate for an open and multipolar cooperation, and the nation aligns them through ASEAN-led mechanisms that are central to its Indo-Pacific vision. He noted that the region is witnessing rapid changes in the face of growing strategic competition and pressure & uncertainty created at times through actions at sea, in addition to threats such as terrorism, cybercrime, piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing, climate-related disasters and risks to vital supply chains. No country alone can address these challenges, he said.
Shri Rajnath Singh underlined the need to discuss differences early and peacefully, before they become disputes, and pitched for a regional order where countries work together without being forced to choose sides. “India believes that security is strengthened when countries build capacity together, respect international law and maintain trust through dialogue,” he said.
Raksha Mantri highlighted the centuries-old close ties between India and Southeast Asia rooted in shared history, culture, trade & ideas, reiterating that the Act East Policy is a long-term commitment to working with the region as an equal partner. “India’s approach and ASEAN’s outlook on the Indo-Pacific can complement each other. We should strengthen cooperation, not create competition between regional forums,” he said.
Shri Rajnath Singh stated that keeping the Indian Ocean and the waters of Southeast Asia safe is a shared responsibility as they are part of one connected maritime space, crucial for trade, energy, people and essential goods. Strengthening maritime domain awareness, interoperability, and collaboration in underwater awareness will be key to ensuring a stable, rule-based maritime order, he said.
Raksha Mantri stressed that as 2026 has been designated as ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation, it is an opportunity to turn shared interest into practical action. “We should improve the sharing of maritime information, strengthen cooperation among our navies and coast guards, and build the ability to respond together to emergencies. We should also work against piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing and other threats, in accordance with international law,” he said.
Terming defence technology as another crucial area, Shri Rajnath Singh pointed out that Artificial Intelligence, drones, cyber capabilities and space-based systems are becoming increasingly important, with recent conflicts demonstrating that relatively low-cost drones can challenge expensive defence systems. He underscored the need to respond with practical, affordable and adaptable solutions.
“India believes that innovation should not remain limited to a few large organisations. Start-ups, universities, research institutions and smaller companies can all contribute. India’s initiatives like Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) and Technology Development Fund (TDF) have created a way to collaborate with innovators for our defence needs,” stated Raksha Mantri as he called for exploring ways for innovators to work together on clearly defined problems, such as counter-drone systems, cyber defence, maritime surveillance and disaster response.
Shri Rajnath Singh called for joint research projects, shared testing opportunities, exchanges among young researchers and carefully designed innovation challenges, emphasising that such cooperation must also protect sensitive information, respect intellectual property and ensure that technology is shared responsibly. “The aim should be to develop useful capabilities while strengthening trust between our countries,” he said.
On defence industrial cooperation, Raksha Mantri asserted that India is ready to explore cooperation with ASEAN partners in areas such as patrol vessels, radars, air-defence systems, helicopters, drones and other technologies, according to each country’s needs and priorities. He said the ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ initiative focuses on building stronger domestic capabilities, but self-reliance does not mean working in isolation. It can create opportunities for trusted partners to design, build, maintain and improve equipment together, he said.
Underlining the importance of co-development, co-production, maintenance, repair and overhaul, training and long-term technical support, Shri Rajnath Singh said these arrangements can build local skills, support industry and make supply chains more reliable.  “Our researchers need to look closely at what makes such partnerships work: clear requirements, reliable after-sales support, appropriate technology safeguards, fair sharing of responsibilities and benefits, and opportunities for local companies and skilled workers. Our goal should be lasting partnerships, not one-time transactions,” he said.
Calling for enhanced cooperation to deal with natural disasters, Raksha Mantri stated that Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) should be a regular part of defence dialogue as cyclones, floods, rising sea levels and extreme weather can damage ports, disrupt trade and threaten lives and livelihoods. “We can learn from one another, share best practices and improve coordination before a crisis occurs,” he said.
On the crucial role of Think Tanks, Shri Rajnath Singh said Governments need good analysis, but they also need ideas that can be put into practice. He suggested some practical outcomes from the forum, including development of a joint India-ASEAN research agenda on maritime security, cyber threats, emerging technologies, disaster response and defence-industry cooperation; regular exchanges among researchers, including young scholars, through fellowships, visiting programmes and joint publications; Identification of a small number of pilot projects such as a tabletop exercise on maritime disaster response, a joint study on counter-drone solutions, or a research project on secure maritime information sharing; Promotion of Track 1.5 and Track 2 dialogues for researchers, practitioners and policymakers to continue their discussions between formal meetings; and preparing a concise set of recommendations, identifying institutions that could take them forward, and reviewing progress at a future meeting.
In his welcome address, Director General, MP-IDSA Amb Sujan R Chinoy expressed gratitude to Raksha Mantri for his vision and support in strengthening India’s defence and security partnerships with ASEAN. Welcoming participants from all eleven ASEAN member states and India, he described the forum as an important institutional milestone in the evolution of ASEAN-India defence engagement. He expressed confidence that the forum would institutionalise enduring dialogue between India and ASEAN’s strategic communities and help identify practical areas for deeper defence and security cooperation.
About ASEAN - India Defence Think Tank Forum
Being held on October 14 & 15, 2026, the forum aims to strengthen strategic dialogue, promote joint analysis and identify practical avenues for enhanced defence and security cooperation between India and ASEAN. The initiative follows the announcement made by Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh during the second ASEAN-India Defence Ministers’ Informal Meeting in Kuala Lumpur on October 31, 2025, on the sidelines of the 12th ADMM-Plus.
Across a two-day programme, the forum will deliberate on strategic stability, regional geopolitics, maritime security, grey-zone challenges, HADR, maritime domain awareness, defence technology, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, space, unmanned systems, defence industry collaboration and resilient supply chains. The discussions are expected to contribute to a stronger and more forward-looking ASEAN-India defence partnership.

He encouraged banks to proactively examine viable loan proposals from farmers, MSMEs, women entrepreneurs and tourism enterprises.
Dr Sukanta Majumdar pointed out that 2,574 villages are yet to be covered. Of these, 2,515 are to be connected through India Post Payments Bank and 59 through physical bank branches. He urged State Governments and banks to set clear deadlines and speed up the expansion of banking services.
The Union Minister of State identified the lack of suitable buildings, all-weather roads and VSAT or fibre connectivity as major challenges. He urged Chief Secretaries to assign clear responsibilities and timelines for every pending location. He also asked banks to operationalise prepared locations quickly and deploy Business Correspondents and BC-Sakhis wherever full-fledged branches are not feasible.

The four breakout sessions at the conclave focused on banking infrastructure, MSMEs and women entrepreneurs, agricultural finance, and infrastructure financing.
Union MoS Dr Sukanta Majumdar said that, under the guidance of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the Central Government continues to address policy barriers and monitor progress on the banking roadmap. He also acknowledged the guidance of Union Minister for Development of North Eastern Region  Jyotiraditya M. Scindia in advancing the region's development.

title: Central Government approves India’s accession to Southern Indian Ocean Fisheries Agreement (SIOFA)
subtitle: Accession to strengthen India’s presence in High Seas fisheries, expand access to high-value marine resources and enhance participation in global fisheries governance
ministry: Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                14 OCT 2026 5:18PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Central Government has approved India’s accession to the
Southern Indian Ocean Fisheries Agreement (SIOFA)
, representing a strategic milestone that reinforces India’s position in global fisheries governance. Subsequent to Guidelines for High Sea Fisheries issued in December, 2025 by Government of India, this initiative would provide a regional framework to expand India’s fishing fleet into international waters. Consequently, India will be positioned to safeguard its strategic interests, broaden economic opportunities, and establish legitimate rights for the sustainable harvesting of high-value marine resources under the SIOFA framework. Furthermore, it affirms a recognized presence on the high seas and advances India’s Blue Economy in alignment with national economic, scientific, and strategic priorities.
With India’s accession to SIOFA, Indian-flagged fishing vessels and enterprises will be able to undertake authorised fishing of squids, toothfish, alfonsino, and other non-migratory fish stocks within SIOFA's jurisdiction.
Accession to SIOFA will further enable India to collaborate with other Cooperating Parties to advance the objectives of the Agreement,
namely
, scientific understanding and sustainable harvest of High Seas resources, participation in the scientific assessments of the resources covered under the Agreement, and prevention of illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.
Accession will also advance India's strategic regional priorities and strengthen national coastal security through active involvement in the High Seas Boarding and Inspection (HSBI) Scheme, which has been adopted and is set to be implemented under the SIOFA.
Currently, India, as a Cooperating Non-Contracting Party (CNCP) to the SIOFA, has limited participation in decision-making, including in key bodies such as the Scientific Committee and the Compliance Committee. Accession as a Contracting Party would enable India to participate fully in these bodies and provide access to scientific data, research programmes, and stock assessments. It will open up new fishing opportunities for the Indian fishers and entrepreneurs. India's active contribution to sustainable fishing practices in the SIOFA region will also play a key role in preserving marine resources, ensuring their long-term viability and supporting the livelihoods of Indian fishing communities.
Backgrounder:
The High Seas constitute approximately 65% of the global ocean and are currently dominated by five countries/regions: China (21%), Taiwan (13%), Japan (11%), South Korea (11%), and Spain (8%). There are two major
Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (RFMOs)
in the Indian Ocean, viz. the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) and the Southern Indian Ocean Fisheries Agreement (SIOFA). India has been a Contracting Party to the IOTC since 1996, which regulates highly migratory tuna and tuna-like species.
India has been a cooperating non-Contracting Party (CNCP) of SIOFA, since 2022. With this membership, India secures legitimate fishing rights, access to marine resources in the High Seas under the SIOFA’s area of competence, and the opportunity to establish a recognized presence alongside existing global fleets. This Agreement covers fishery resources including fish, molluscs, crustaceans, and other sedentary species within the area, but excludes highly migratory species (Annex I of UNCLOS) and the sedentary species which are subject to the fishery jurisdiction of coastal states (Article 77(4) of UNCLOS).
Indian fishing vessels currently operate largely within 60–80 NM of the EEZ, and India needs to develop and expand its fishing capacity across all possible High Seas areas, including through access agreements in other countries' EEZs, thereby contributing to the national exchequer.

title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on Strategic Restructuring of IDBI Bank Ltd.
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                14 OCT 2026 4:51PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Q1.  Who is the Strategic Buyer for the IDBI Bank Ltd.?
Answer:
M/s 10955230 Canada Inc. (parent entity M/s Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd.) has been approved as the Strategic Buyer for the IDBI Bank Ltd.
Q2.  What is the size of this Transaction?
Answer:
The purchase consideration for this transaction is
Rs.52,878.0806181 Crores (in words Rupees Fifty-Two Thousand Eight Hundred Seventy-Eight Crore Eight Lakh Six Thousand and One Hundred Eighty-One only).
Q3.  How will it be split between the Government of India (GoI) and the Life Insurance corporation of India (LIC)?
Answer:
60.72% stake out of the total shareholding of the IDBI Bank Ltd is being sold through this transaction, comprising 30.48% shareholding held by the Gol and 30.24% shareholding held by the LIC. The proceeds will be divided in the same proportion.
Q4.  How many entities were involved in the bidding process?
Answer:
Of the five parties who initially submitted their Expression of interest, four parties qualified as per the eligibility criteria and disqualification conditions prescribed in the Preliminary Information Memorandum (PIM), of which, two finally submitted their techno- financial bids and became Qualified Bidders (QBs) for this transaction.
Q5.  What methodologies were used for the valuation of IDBI Bank Ltd.?
Answer:
The fair value of the enterprise was determined using two alternate methodologies, namely the Market Multiple Method and the Asset Valuation Method.
Q6.  Who carried out the valuation exercise?
Answer:
The valuation of enterprise was carried out by two independent, professional valuation agencies appointed for the purpose. Their names cannot be disclosed due to confidential guarantees enshrined in the process.
Q7.  What role did the stock market price play in the valuation of the IDBI Bank?
Answer:
The volatile stock market price of the narrowly traded IDBI stock fluctuated both above and below the bid offer price (low high range of Rs.61.01 to Rs.118.38 over the valuation period). It was disregarded, as it tended to misalign the valuation with the intrinsic value of the enterprise, and instead, relative valuation by the market multiple method, which overcomes this problem, was used to determine the fair market value of the enterprise based on the 31st March, 2026 closing accounts for all public sector banks.
Q8.  How have the assets, including land and properties, been valued for the IDBI Bank?
Answers:
The Asset Valuation Method, which considered both tangible and intangible assets, including land and properties, along with the liabilities, was used to determine the fair net asset value of the enterprise as per the 31st March, 2026 audited accounts of the IDBI Bank.
Q9.  What was the benchmark price used for this transaction?
Answer:
The average of the two independent valuations (Rs.75.99 per share) served as the benchmark price for the evaluation of the qualified bids. The winning bid was found to be higher than the benchmark price as well as the fair value estimates of both the independent valuation agencies.
Q10.  How was the benchmark price determined?
Answer:
The benchmark price was the average of the fair market value determined by the Market Multiple Method and the fair net asset value determined by the Asset Valuation Method.
Q11.  What is the further course of action?
Answer:
The Successful Bidder would now present its credentials to the RBI in accordance with the ‘Fit & Proper’ assessment conducted at the EoI stage and submit a roadmap for the compliance of regulatory conditions prescribed therein.
Q12.    What is the residual equity stake left with the GoI and the LIC?
Answer:
GoI will retain 15% residual equity stake while the LIC will retain 19% equity stake. Both of them will withdraw their nominees from the Board and become public shareholders.
Q13.    How will the GoI and LIC dissolve their residual shareholding in the IDBI Bank?
Answer:
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has delegated powers to the Alternative Mechanism to undertake minority stake sales of the residual GoI shareholding through the open market in accordance with the standard operating procedure. The LIC will be free to manage its residual shareholding in accordance with its internal procedures while ensuring compliance with the direction of its regulators.
Q14.    What impact will it have on the banking sector and the economy at large?
Answer:
It will have a significantly positive effect on the banking and financial sector of our economy. The IDBI Bank, post-privatization, would be able to generate funds without any dependence on government assistance as has been the experience in the past. It is expected that the strategic buyer will infuse private capital, bring-in new technology and better management practices, which will help enhance its business potential and make it more competitive for both credit and deposit growth.
Q15. What impact will it have on India’s external sector at the time of geo-political strain?
Answer:
It will be the largest FDI in the financial sector of our economy so far, and will help generate a positive sentiment for economic reforms, while improving the investment climate in the country at large.

title: Government Approves Strategic Restructuring of IDBI Bank Ltd.
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                14 OCT 2026 4:50PM by PIB Delhi
content:
IDBI Bank Ltd. is a scheduled commercial bank regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Due to its poor financial health, the Bank required repeated infusion of capital, initially provided by the Government of India and later by the LIC. On 5th May, 2017, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) put the IDBI Bank under the Prompt Corrective Action Framework and imposed several restrictions in view of its non-performing assets and losses incurred by the Bank. After considering the improvement in the Bank’s financial health, the RBI later, vide its letter dated 10th March, 2021, lifted the restrictions imposed on the IDBI Bank subject to certain conditions and continuous monitoring.
It was against this backdrop that the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) approved strategic restructuring of the IDBI Bank Ltd., and in compliance thereof, it was decided that an aggregate 60.72% of the equity stake in the IDBI Bank Ltd be sold to a Strategic Buyer, of which, the GoI share would be 30.48% and the LIC share would be 30.24%, leaving a residual shareholding of 15% with the GoI and 19% with the LIC.
The decision of the CCEA was implemented through a two-stage, competitive bidding process supported by a multi-layered, collective decision-making mechanism consisting of the Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG), the Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment (CGD) and the Alternative Mechanism (AM) consisting of an empowered Group of Cabinet Ministers.
The Preliminary Information Memorandum (PIM) inviting Expression of Interest (EoI) from all interested parties was issued on 07.10.2022. Only the parties found ‘Fit and Proper’ by the RBI and granted security clearance by the MHA could participate in the bidding stage, for which a Request for Proposal was issued for inviting technical and financial bids from the Qualified Interested Parties (QIPs). Of the five parties who initially submitted their expression of interest, four parties qualified as per the eligibility criteria and disqualification conditions prescribed therein, of which, two finally submitted their techno-financial bids and became Qualified Bidders (QBs) for this Transaction.
After comprehensive evaluation by the CGD and after considering the recommendations of the Alternative Mechanism, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) in its meeting held on 14/10/2026 approved M/s 10955230 Canada Inc. (parent entity M/s Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd.) as the Strategic Buyer for this Transaction for a purchase consideration of Rs.52,878.0806181 Crores (in words Rupees Fifty-Two Thousand Eight Hundred Seventy-Eight Crore Eight Lakh Six Thousand and One Hundred Eighty-One only) for the acquisition of 60.72% stake in the IDBI Bank Ltd, comprising 30.48% equity shareholding held by the Gol and 30.24% equity shareholding held by the LIC.
In such transactions, there is no
a-priori
benchmark for bidding. The bidders do their own valuation and submit their bids in sealed envelopes in a confidential manner. Independent agencies are hired to do a fair valuation of the enterprise contemporaneously, which is then used as a comparator to assess the reasonableness of the bids submitted.
Under this transaction, the initial bids were invited in the financial year 2025-26. For comparison, a reserve price of Rs.94.42 per share was fixed at that time, which was directly and indirectly influenced by the impacted market price. The unimpacted counter-factual was not visible at that time, except that the unimpacted pre-EoI price of the IDBI stock was Rs.42.40 per share on the last trading day before the issue of the PIM/EoI on 07.10.2022. In contrast, the impacted price was Rs.108.12 per share on the last trading day before the invitation of initial bids on 08.01.2026. The initial bids fell short of the reserve price arrived at that time and were not approved. When it became known that the initial bids have not succeeded, the impacted stock market price itself corrected, and fell significantly below the discovered bid price of Rs.75 per share.
Subsequently, in exercise of the powers delegated and conferred upon the collective decision-making mechanism, and to enhance the value of the transaction as far as possible, sealed bids reflecting their best offers were invited from the qualified bidders in the financial year 2026-27. The stock price of the IDBI Stock was Rs.70.38 per share on the trading day last before the invitation of best offer bids on 18.05.2026.
The stock market price of the narrowly traded IDBI stock continued to be volatile and fluctuated both above and below the bid discovered price with a high-low range of Rs.118.38 to Rs.61.01 per share over the valuation period. The stock market price was consequently disregarded, as it tended to misalign valuation with the intrinsic value of the enterprise. Instead, Relative Valuation by the Market Multiple Method, which overcomes this problem, was used to determine the fair market value of the enterprise on the basis of 31st March, 2026 closing accounts of all public sector banks. Additionally, the Asset Valuation Method, which considers both tangible and intangible assets, including land and properties along with the liabilities, was used to determine the fair net asset value of the enterprise as per the 31st March, 2026 audited accounts of the IDBI Bank Ltd.
Accordingly, the fair valuation of the enterprise was carried out by two professional valuation agencies using two independent methodologies as explained above. The average of these fair valuations was Rs.75.99 per share, which served as the benchmark price for the evaluation of the qualified bids. Since the winning best offer bid of Rs.81 per share was above the benchmark price, as well as fair value estimates of both the independent valuation agencies, it was adjudged to be reasonable and approved.
The successful bidder will be required to present its credentials to the Reserve Bank of India in accordance with the Fit and Proper Assessment conducted at the EoI stage and submit its roadmap for the compliance of regulatory conditions prescribed therein. Once completed, this will be the largest FDI in the financial sector of our economy so far.
The CCEA has also delegated powers to the Alternative Mechanism to undertake minority stake sales of the GoI residual shareholding (15% of the total shareholding of the IDBI Bank Ltd.) through the open market in accordance with the standard operating procedure. The LIC will be free to manage its residual shareholding in accordance with its internal procedures while ensuring compliance with the directions of its regulators.

title: DRI busts illegal import of more than 73,00,000 kg of Pakistan-origin rock salt; four arrested
subtitle: Operation Deep Manifest exposes a transnational smuggling network modus operandi to circumvent India’s import prohibition on Pakistani goods
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                14 OCT 2026 4:09PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) has once again unearthed a large-scale scheme to circumvent India’s prohibition on the import of goods originating in or exported from Pakistan. Under “Operation Deep Manifest”.
DRI detected the import of
295 containers carrying 7,311 metric tonnes of Pakistan-origin Industrial/Himalayan Rock Salt
, with an estimated market value of around Rs. 30 crore. The consignments were routed through Colombo Port, Sri Lanka, and falsifying their origin by using fabricated certificates of origin and invoices issued by UAE-based entities.
Acting on specific intelligence, DRI launched a coordinated, fortnight-long operation between 26 September and 11 October 2026, conducting searches at linked premises in Gandhidham, Adipur, Veraval, Panipat, Pune, Patiala, Delhi and Mumbai.
Investigation revealed that nine importers had brought in the 295 containers through Mundra and Kandla ports since March 2026, in violation of the prohibition. Out of the total 295 containers detected, five containers carrying 140 MT of Industrial/Himalayan Rock Salt, valued at Rs. 24.41 lakh, have been seized at Kandla Port. In addition, sales proceeds amounting to Rs. 20.96 lakh held in the importers’ bank accounts have been seized.
Preliminary investigation has uncovered a transnational network involving entities owned by Pakistani, UAE, Sri Lankan and Indian nationals. The network allegedly coordinated the shipments and supporting documentation to disguise the Pakistani origin of the goods. Fabricated invoices issued by Dubai-based firms were used to support the transactions. Significantly, Bills of Lading relating to the Pakistan–Sri Lanka leg of the shipments and customs declarations filed with Sri Lanka Customs expressly mentioned Pakistan as the country of origin and India as the final destination. The Certificates of Origin submitted by the importers were found to be fabricated.
Four persons have been arrested under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962: two proprietors/partners of importing firms, a Customs Broker’s G-card holder, and the owner of a Dubai-based supplier who had also established and operated an importing firm in his father’s name.
In a similar crackdown last month, DRI seized over 362,000 kg of Pakistan-origin dry dates packed in 13 containers imported by a Mumbai-based firm at CFS Ambad, Nashik.
These cases highlight the evolving methods used by transnational networks to circumvent India’s import prohibition on Pakistani origin goods through third-country routing, false declarations of origin, fabricated trade documents and opaque financial arrangements. DRI remains committed to identifying and dismantling such networks and safeguarding India’s economic and national security interests.
Following the Pahalgam terror attack in April 2025, the Government of India imposed a complete prohibition on the direct or indirect import or transit of all goods originating in or exported from Pakistan, in the interest of national security and public policy, vide DGFT Notification No. 06/2025-26 dated 02.05.2025.

.

To study the possible causes of such demographic changes, such as variations in fertility, cross border movement (including illegal immigration), economic opportunities, and other socioenvironmental factors.
To identify the underlying factors behind these changes, including illegal immigration, abnormal settlement patterns, and planned migration.
To analyze structural population changes at the level of religious or social communities, especially those diverging from uniform trends.
To recommend a well-organized and permanent operational system for the legal, fair and time bound identification, detention, and deportation of illegal immigrants already residing in the country.
To recommend an appropriate institutional mechanism to strengthen border management, population stabilization, and identification systems for sustained monitoring of such trends.
To propose a comprehensive policy framework to enhance coordination between Central and State Governments in matters related to illegal immigration and resultant demographic imbalance.
The Committee may recommend any other measure it deems appropriate to address the challenges arising from demographic changes, including due to illegal immigration.

title: As A Follow-Up to The Departmental Summit on Water 2026, Department Of Drinking Water and Sanitation Organised Virtual Conference On Convergence Of JJM 2.0 With VB-G RAM G For Source Sustainability And Gram Panchayat-Led Water Governance
subtitle: Secretary DDWS calls for scientific planning through DSS and Yuktdhara, prioritisation of critical drinking water sources and stronger inter-departmental convergence
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                14 OCT 2026 4:15PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The
Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti
, today organised the
third virtual conference with States and Union Territories
as part of a series of thematic consultations being held in follow-up to the
Departmental Summit on Water 2026 held on 1-2 September 2026
. The conference focused on strengthening convergence between
Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0
and
VB-G RAM G
to advance source sustainability, water security and Gram Panchayat-led planning for sustainable rural drinking water service delivery.
The virtual conference brought together senior officials from State PHEDs/Rural Water Supply Departments, Rural Development Departments, Panchayati Raj Departments and representatives from the Ministries of Rural Development and Panchayati Raj, Government of India. States rural water supply departments including Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, and Rajasthan shared their experiences and initiatives on source sustainability, operation and maintenance of water supply assets and use of digital planning tools.
Addressing in the conference,
Shri Ashok K.K. Meena, Secretary, DDWS
, said that while Jal Jeevan Mission has enabled the creation of extensive rural drinking water infrastructure across the country, the focus of JJM 2.0 shifts towards ensuring long-term functionality, reliability and sustainability of these assets. He emphasised that sustainable drinking water services can only be ensured through systematic protection, recharge and management of drinking water sources alongside regular maintenance of infrastructure.
Highlighting the opportunities available through VB-G RAM G, the Secretary stated that the programme provides a strong framework for undertaking water conservation, groundwater recharge, source sustainability and maintenance-related interventions that directly contribute to drinking water security. He stressed that convergence should focus on two key objectives - sustainability of drinking water sources and continued functionality of infrastructure created under Jal Jeevan Mission.
The Secretary underscored the need for integrating
JJM Village Action Plans and Source Sustainability Plans
with the
Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans (VGPPs)
and ensuring their incorporation into the Gram Panchayat Development Plan (GPDP) process. He stated that water security interventions should emerge from scientific assessment of local water resources and be approved through the Gram Sabha to enable community ownership and accountability.
Emphasising the central role of Gram Panchayats in rural water governance, Shri Meena stated that Gram Panchayats, Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs) and local institutions possess critical knowledge regarding water sources, seasonal variations and local requirements. Their active participation in planning, implementation and monitoring is essential for ensuring long-term sustainability of drinking water systems.
He highlighted that the selection of source sustainability works should be based on scientific assessments and local needs. He referred to interventions such as check dams, gully plugs, recharge shafts, injection wells, underground dykes, rooftop rainwater harvesting structures and other groundwater recharge measures that can be undertaken based on local hydrogeological conditions. He urged States to utilise the
Decision Support System (DSS)
developed under JJM 2.0 and the
Yuktdhara Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)
for identifying vulnerable drinking water sources and scientifically prioritising interventions.
Calling for stronger institutional coordination, the Secretary directed States to establish clear mechanisms for technical scrutiny, approval, implementation and monitoring of convergence works. He emphasised the importance of coordinated action among Rural Water Supply, Rural Development and Panchayati Raj Departments at the State, district and Gram Panchayat levels, supported by institutional platforms such as District Water and Sanitation Missions (DWSMs), State Water and Sanitation Missions (SWSMs) and State-level Apex Committees.
The Secretary identified five priority outcomes for States and UTs: alignment of JJM plans with Gram Panchayat plans under VB-G RAM G; scientific identification of source sustainability works using DSS and Yuktdhara; establishment of technical scrutiny and approval mechanisms; seamless inter-departmental data sharing; and creation of joint monitoring systems for tracking both physical progress and water security outcomes.
Ms. Deeksha S. Bisht, Assistant Commissioner, Ministry of Rural Development
made a detailed presentation on the scope of convergence under VB-G RAM G and JJM for the planning framework for strengthening water security. She informed that the programme provides 128 water security-related works covering groundwater recharge, rainwater harvesting, watershed treatment, rejuvenation of water bodies, source sustainability and maintenance of water-related assets. She highlighted that water security continues to be a major focus area under VB-G RAM G and emphasised the importance of scientific planning, community participation and outcome-based implementation.
Referring to the joint advisories issued by the Ministry of Rural Development and Ministry Jal Shakti, she informed that States have been advised to prioritise water-related works in water-stressed areas based on groundwater stress classifications and local water security requirements. She also highlighted the importance of water budgeting, hydrogeological assessments and geospatial planning tools in identifying appropriate interventions and ensuring optimal utilisation of resources.
On planning convergence, Ms Bisht informed that annual plans prepared under the Viksit Gram Panchayat Planning framework would be integrated with the Gram Panchayat Development Plan (GPDP) process to enable a unified planning approach at the Gram Panchayat level. The discussion further emphasised the need to prioritise drinking water sources identified through the Decision Support System (DSS) and incorporate such information into village-level planning and implementation processes.
The State of
Odisha
shared its experience in implementing large-scale water conservation and source sustainability interventions through convergence and highlighted initiatives relating to groundwater recharge, greywater management, catchment treatment, source protection and climate-resilient water infrastructure. Odisha also presented examples of recharge structures, community recharge pits and restoration of traditional water bodies being implemented to strengthen drinking water security.
The State of
Madhya Pradesh
presented its initiatives to operationalise provisions under the O&M Rules, 2026, and facilitate maintenance of rural water supply schemes through Gram Panchayats. The State highlighted model estimates for rainwater harvesting, recharge structures and source sustainability works while also sharing institutional mechanisms established for improving coordination between Rural Development and Rural Water Supply Departments.
Rajasthan
presented a framework for preventive, corrective and emergency maintenance of rural water supply infrastructure through convergence with VB-G RAM G. The State highlighted the role of Gram Panchayats, Paani Samitis and PHED functionaries in ensuring regular maintenance and sustained functionality of water supply assets.
Shri Sumit Priyadarshi, Deputy Advisor, NJJM made a detail presentation on
Implementation of the Decision Support System (DSS) for Source Sustainability and Mitigation of Drinking-Water Risks
. He said that the Decision Support System (DSS) is a key tool for identifying vulnerable drinking water sources facing water quality and water quantity risks. States were urged to utilise DSS data for prioritising interventions in habitations, validating risks through field assessments and monitoring outcomes following implementation of mitigation measures.
The State of
Assam
shared its experience in using DSS for identification and verification of water-quantity stressed villages and highlighted efforts relating to GIS mapping, field verification, development of standard operating procedures and preparation of remedial action plans for vulnerable drinking water sources.
Presenting the concluding remarks,
Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, Additional Secretary & Mission Director, National Jal Jeevan Mission
, stressed that States must ensure that investments under VB-G RAM G are directed towards addressing drinking water challenges identified through the DSS. Referring to the water-security advisories issued jointly by the Ministries of Jal Shakti and Rural Development, he noted that expenditure on water-related works in identified water-stressed blocks needs to translate expenditure into measurable improvements in drinking water security.
He informed that efforts were underway to integrate information relating to drinking water sources and associated Gram Panchayats into the Rural Development MIS so that planning, expenditure and implementation of water-related works could be monitored more effectively. He urged States and UTs to ensure that
District Collectors, Chief Executive Officers of Zila Panchayats and relevant field functionaries actively utilise DSS data for identifying and prioritising vulnerable drinking water sources facing water quality and water quantity risks
.
Shri Soan also called upon States to undertake post-monsoon assessment and testing of drinking water sources, validate water source conditions through field verification and prepare suitable mitigation plans. He emphasised the need for close coordination among Rural Water Supply, Rural Development and Panchayati Raj Departments to ensure that source sustainability interventions are scientifically planned, properly monitored and aligned with local requirements.
He further urged States to issue necessary advisories to district and field-level officials, prioritise interventions in water-stressed areas, and prepare concrete action plans for presentation during the regional conferences scheduled from November 2026. He reiterated that the ultimate objective of the convergence framework is not merely creation of assets, but ensuring long-term sustainability of drinking water sources and reliable rural drinking water services through coordinated institutional action and strengthened Gram Panchayat-led governance.
The conference concluded with a shared commitment by the Centre and States/UTs to operationalise the agreed convergence framework and accelerate implementation of source sustainability interventions under Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 and VB-G RAM G.

It was also highlighted to the NLUs that they may effectively utilize their pro bono clubs, researchers and students to carry out the ground level analysis  of case pendency in the selected districts and suggest possible strategies to address the issue. As the way forward, NLUs were requested to develop focused approach for the 100 districts, based on district-specific diagnosis and identify the main causes of delay. They were also requested to suggest feasible mechanism to reduce litigation pendency. title: India’s Coir Sector: Creating Livelihoods, Promoting Entrepreneurship and Driving Sustainable Growth
subtitle:
Over 21,000 coir units are registered on the Udyam registration portal, generating employment for 2.3 lakh people

Exports of coir products witnessed an increase of 305% in the last 10 years
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                14 OCT 2026 10:09AM by PIB Delhi
content:
India, the world’s largest producer and exporter of coir, is rooted in tradition and driven by innovation. The coir sector is emerging as a vibrant, eco-friendly and sustainable driver of economic and social progress.  It not only promotes the productive use of coconut husks but also generates livelihoods and supports the growth of rural and traditional communities. With its strong focus on sustainability, value addition and inclusive growth, the Coir sector is playing a crucial role in India’s journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047.
Made from coir, eco-friendly and sustainable products like mats, mattresses, ropes, brushes and other utility items are increasingly becoming a part of our everyday lives. But what exactly is coir?
Coir is a natural, fibrous material extracted from the outer, tough husk of coconuts. These natural fibres are processed and transformed into a wide range of commercial products. The Coir Sector, one of India’s oldest and traditional industries, represents an eco-friendly manufacturing sector that extracts, processes and converts coconut husk fibres into value-added products.
Coir sector in India:-
India is the world’s largest producer and exporter of coir and coir products, accounting for about two-thirds of global production. The Indian Coir Industry has a turnover of approximately ₹16,000 crore and contributes close to 1% to India’s GDP.
In FY 2025-26, India’s exports of coir and coir products were valued at ₹6,614.40 crore, with the US, China, Netherlands, Spain and the UK being the major export destinations. Coir pith, fibre, yarn and tufted mats are the major coir products exported by India.
The Indian Coir Sector has more than 21,000 coir units and provides direct and indirect employment to over 7 lakh workers, with 80% being women from rural households.
The Ministry of MSME runs a central sector scheme, “Coir Vikas Yojana (CVY)”, aimed at promoting the sustainable development and growth of the Coir Sector and providing support to coir artisans and the coir industry.
The CVY focuses on:
Development of new technologies, machines & products for Coir Industry.
Conducting skill training and promotional programmes
Promotion of sales of coir and coir products in domestic as well as international markets.
Creating awareness through publicity activities and participation in trade fairs, expos, etc.
Providing financial assistance to promote sales.
Facilitating the participation of coir exporters in international exhibitions.
Compiling and publishing statistics on the coir sector.
Key achievements during last 12 years (since 2014-15):
More than 21,000 coir units are registered on the Udyam registration portal employing 2.3 lakh persons making them a part of the formal MSME policy ecosystem.
Export of coir and coir products has more than quadrupled, from ₹1,630.33 crore in FY 2014-15 to ₹6,614.40 crore in FY 2025-26, registering an increase of 305.70%.
Over 68,000 persons have been trained under various training programmes with more than 80% being women.
More than 150 innovative machines, technologies and value-added coir products in the coir sector.
Facilitated participation of more than 1,000 exporters in International Exhibitions abroad and financial assistance of more than ₹20 crores given to more than 850 entrepreneurs under Export Market Promotion.
1,400+ promotional programmes organised and 950+ exhibitions participated across India.
Coir Giving Wings to Dreams: Inspiring Stories of Enterprise & Success
Smt. Ranjana Ramchandra Kadam, from Sindhudurg district, Maharashtra, turned her entrepreneurial dream into reality under the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP), which enabled her to establish a coir unit with guidance from the Coir Board. She constructed a shed and procured the necessary machinery and equipment to start her business, with significant support from the Coir Board office. Her factory currently manufactures coir ropes, pillows and doormats. Through this venture, she has provided full-time employment to six people.
Sampoorna Plus Agro Fertilizer Enterprises, Kozhikode, Kerala, under Shri Surendran P., was strengthened through the training and technical guidance provided by the Coir Board, Sub-Regional Office, Kannur and the Central Coir Research Institute (CCRI), Kalavoor. He actively participated in hands-on training programmes, demonstrations, and awareness sessions on the production and effective utilisation of coir pith bio-fertiliser. Within a short period of one year, his enterprise has successfully built a customer base of more than 500 customers. The unit has also recorded impressive sales of more than 20 tonnes of coir pith bio-fertiliser. The enterprise currently provides employment to 5 workers, including 2 women workers.
3.   Smt. Allam Gowthamy from East Godavari District, Andhra Pradesh, five years ago underwent training at the Coir Board Training Centre. Motivated by the technical guidance she established her own enterprise, Adigo Coir Products. She availed financial assistance under the PMEGP. Today, the unit has achieved an annual turnover of approximately ₹35 lakh and generates an annual profit of around ₹10 lakh. The enterprise has also created employment for six women. She also actively conducting training programmes with the support of the Coir Board Regional Office, Rajahmundry and Mandal Parishat authorities, and nearly 120 women have been trained in coir mat weaving, rope making and handicraft production.
4.  Shri G. Sabu, from Alappuzha, Kerala, has started the Coir spinning unit in the year 2024 under the PMEGP scheme and through Coir Board Regional Office, Kalavoor. Within two years of operation, the unit achieved steady production of coir yarn and rope supplied to local coir societies and manufacturers in Alappuzha. The enterprise generated direct employment for 8–10 local workers, predominantly women from nearby villages. The monthly turnover increased substantially, providing the entrepreneur with a stable income and creating regular wages for employees.

title: CEA Brainstorming Event: Making Indian Power Sector AI Enabled (International Conference cum Exhibition)
date:

content:
Under the theme “Making Indian Power Sector AI Enabled”, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) held the
first day
of its two-day international conference-cum-exhibition at Manekshaw Centre, New Delhi, on 14 October 2026.
Shri Manohar Lal, Union Minister for Power and Housing & Urban Affairs and Shri Prahlad Joshi, Union Minister of Education, Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution & New and Renewable Energy Government of India, conveyed their messages on the occasion. Shri Shripad Yesso Naik, Union Minister of State for Power and New & Renewable Energy; Shri Jitin Prasada, Union Minister of State for Commerce & Industry and Electronics & Information Technology; Shri Pankaj Agarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Power; Shri Ghanshyam Prasad, Chairperson, CEA ; Shri Mayank Tewari, Additional Secretary, Ministry of New and Renewable Energy; were also present during inauguration.
The inaugural session featured addresses by senior government dignitaries and the leadership of CEA. Shri Pankaj Agarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Power and Shri Mayank Tewari, Additional Secretary, Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, addressed the gathering, highlighting the importance of advancing India’s power sector in response to emerging challenges and technological developments. Further, Shri Ghanshyam Prasad, Chairperson, CEA, set the context for the conference. It was highlighted that CEA has already formed a team of 54 artificial intelligence (AI) enthusiast/ brand ambassador. They will take it forward in all areas of power sector. All power utilities may also have dedicated AI team.
The session also saw the launch of CEA’s Vidhyut Dwar Portal and the release of the CEA Manual on Transmission Planning Criteria, 2026. The CEA Employee Awards were also distributed during the session, recognising outstanding performance and exceptional contributions by CEA employees.
The event brought together stakeholders from the power sector to deliberate on practical applications of AI across generation, regulation, renewable energy integration, transmission and distribution systems. The technical programme on Day 1 featured six parallel thematic discussions: Optimizing Generation through AI for Conventional Sources; Regulatory Reforms using AI; AI-Enabled Renewable Energy Integration for a Flexible Grid; Modernising Distribution through AI; Transmission Modernization, Grid Stability and System Restoration through AI; and AI-Enabled Rooftop Solar, Microgrids and Mini-Grids.
The session on conventional generation examined how AI may support heat-rate and combustion optimisation, flexible plant operation, predictive maintenance, digital twins, auxiliary-power optimisation and emissions monitoring. These applications may help improve plant availability and operational efficiency while enabling conventional stations to respond more flexibly to changing system requirements as renewable energy expands.
Discussions on regulatory reforms considered the use of AI, advanced analytics and digital tools for reviewing aggregate revenue requirement and tariff filings, validating submissions, organising regulatory knowledge, monitoring compliance and supporting market surveillance. The discussions also highlighted that AI may function as a human-supervised decision-support tool and may not replace statutory judgment, procedural fairness or regulatory accountability.
The session on renewable energy integration explored AI-based forecasting of variable renewable generation and demand, improved visibility of distributed energy resources, storage optimisation, congestion management and coordination of renewable assets through virtual power plants. The focus was on enabling a flexible and reliable grid through better data, forecasting and coordination of resources.
Modernisation of distribution systems was discussed with reference to the growing availability of smart-meter, network and asset data. Potential applications included demand forecasting, power-procurement optimisation, predictive maintenance of distribution transformers, outage detection and fault localisation, energy auditing, loss analytics, billing and revenue assurance, consumer services and regulatory reporting. These applications may support more reliable supply, lower losses and more responsive consumer services.
The discussion on transmission modernisation and grid stability examined AI-enabled network planning, corridor and right-of-way optimisation, drone-based inspection and computer vision, predictive maintenance, digital twins, dynamic line rating, congestion and contingency analysis, inertia forecasting, and decision support for system restoration and black-start preparedness. Participants considered the data, digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, governance and capacity-building requirements that would support adoption at scale.
The session on AI-enabled rooftop solar, microgrids and mini-grids focused on intelligent planning and operation of decentralised energy resources. Topics included rooftop solar identification and sizing, feeder-level forecasting, autonomous microgrid operation, storage optimisation, agriculture-feeder analytics, demand response and aggregation of rooftop solar, batteries, electric vehicles and flexible loads.
Across the discussions, a common theme was the need to move from isolated technology demonstrations towards prioritised, implementable use cases supported by reliable data, interoperability, appropriate safeguards, institutional capability and measurable performance indicators. The deliberations are intended to inform practical pathways for responsible adoption and scaling of AI applications in the Indian power sector.
The two-day brainstorming event is being organised as part of overall initiative aims to develop a coordinated and outcome-oriented approach to AI adoption across the electricity value chain, supporting efficient and flexible power supply, reliable and intelligent networks, responsive institutions, secure digitalisation and resilient domestic industrial capability.

The Union Cabinet chaired by the Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi has approved the proposal of the Department of Rural Development for Continuation of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) with total outlay of Rs. 53,428 crore for five years from 2026-27 to 2030-31 with (i) Renaming of the scheme & sub-schemes (ii) Revision in eligibility criteria, coverage and rate of assistance for divyangjan pension and (iii) continuation of pension schemes for old aged & widows and family benefit scheme in its existing form.
Details:
Renaming of scheme and sub schemes:
Existing Name
Approved name
National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP)

National Family Benefit scheme

Amount of assistance under divyangjan pension scheme will now be Rs.375/- for the age group of 0-79 yrs and Rs.625/- for 80 yrs and above. The following changes have been made along with enhancement of rate of assistance under the scheme:

iii.
Pension schemes for old aged & widows and family benefit scheme will continue in its existing form.
Benefits:
A total of 3.20 crore beneficiaries across all the 36 States/UTs will benefit from this approval.
Implementation strategy and target:

The programme brought together 33 Ambassadors and senior embassy officials representing 29 countries, providing them with first-hand exposure to CSIR's scientific capabilities, indigenous technologies and advanced research infrastructure. The inaugural edition featured visits to two premier CSIR laboratories in New Delhi—the CSIR-Central Road Research Institute (CSIR-CRRI) and the CSIR-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology (CSIR-IGIB).
Jointly conceptualised by CSIR and MEA, the initiative seeks to build stronger scientific and technological linkages with partner countries, particularly across the Global South, by showcasing India's research capabilities and identifying opportunities for collaborative research, technology transfer, capacity building and deployment of innovative solutions addressing shared developmental challenges.

Dr. Chalumuri Ravi Sekhar, Director, CSIR-CRRI, and Dr. Souvik Maiti, Director, CSIR-IGIB, introduced the visiting delegation to their respective institutes' research strengths, technological achievements and contributions in the areas of sustainable infrastructure and healthcare.
At CSIR-CRRI, the delegation witnessed several advanced research facilities and technologies, including the Driving Simulator, Cyclic Load Test Facility, Steel Slag Laboratory, a 3D model of bio-binder technology and drone models. A major highlight was the live demonstration of
Ecofix
, a steel slag-based instant pothole repair mix developed for rapid road maintenance. The demonstration showcased how indigenous technologies can transform industrial waste into valuable resources while offering practical, sustainable and cost-effective solutions for infrastructure development.

The visit offered insights into India's growing capabilities in genomics, biomedical research, precision healthcare and biotechnology, highlighting opportunities for scientific cooperation and capacity building in the healthcare sector.

Discussions explored opportunities for joint research, technology partnerships, knowledge exchange, capacity building and adaptation of Indian technologies to address the specific developmental needs of partner countries.
The inaugural MEA–CSIR Tech Familiarization Programme represents an important step towards translating India's scientific and technological strengths into meaningful international partnerships. By bringing foreign diplomatic representatives directly into CSIR laboratories and facilitating interactions with scientists and technology developers, the initiative provides a platform for identifying practical areas of cooperation and accelerating the adoption of innovative solutions.
The programme is expected to open new avenues for sustained engagement between CSIR and countries of the Global South, reinforcing India's commitment to sharing scientific knowledge, technological expertise and indigenous innovations for inclusive and sustainable development.
